sources.title: TodoMVC behavior reference: precise functional contract

model.vision: A dependable personal todo list a small team can use to capture, finish, and clear their work.
model.mission: Keep every person's list safely on the team's side rather than in their browser, so nothing depends on a single tab or device. Deliver one deliberately small, fixed way of working a list that behaves identically whether a person or the team's agent tooling is using it, and decline anything beyond that well-known reference behavior.

items.name: Caller-protocol volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: the protocols through which callers reach the list behaviors. Today the founder requires an ordinary web API for the team's web app and an MCP surface for the team's agent tooling. WHY volatile: agent-tooling protocols are new and change quickly. MCP has had several breaking revisions to transport, auth and tool-schema conventions within about a year, and the team says it builds 'the way we build everything else here', so its house conventions will move with that. LIKELIHOOD: high. Expect at least one protocol revision or a new caller protocol every 6 to 12 months over the system's life. EFFECT if unencapsulated: every list behavior (capture, reword, discard, complete/reopen, toggle all, clear completed, review, items left) would be written once per protocol. Each protocol change would then ripple into the business behavior, and the mission's promise that people and agents get identical behavior would drift apart. Insulates the behaviors from how they are invoked.

items.name: Presentation-host volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: where and how the list experience is rendered and interacted with. At the same moment, some team members use it as a standalone web app and others use it embedded in a host workspace (an MCP Apps host), where the host owns the frame, sizing, focus and the interaction gestures it allows (the reference contract's Enter, Escape, blur and double-click edit gestures). WHY volatile: host workspaces differ from each other and from a browser tab. The team already runs 'other MCP-hosted UIs', so more hosts are expected. LIKELIHOOD: certain today (two hosts at once) and rising as the team adopts more hosts. EFFECT if unencapsulated: view selection, the current-view indicator, the always-visible items-left count, and reword commit/cancel would be re-implemented per host and would diverge, breaking the 'behaves the same as when used directly' guarantee in the Host workspace definition.

items.name: List-keeping technology volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: the technology and location in which every team member's list is durably kept on the team's side. WHY volatile: the founder requires only that lists survive closing, restarting and switching tab or device, and that they are not kept in the browser. The concrete store is left open and will follow the team's infrastructure. A 'try it out tomorrow' deployment will probably start on a simple store and move to the team's standard managed database if the app is adopted. LIKELIHOOD: medium-high. At least one change of store is expected within 1 to 3 years, and storage choices historically change at about that rate. EFFECT if unencapsulated: append, revise, withdraw, settle completion, sweep completed and recall would each carry store-specific code. A migration would then touch every behavior and put the 'no lost work' guarantee at risk. The guarantee itself is fixed. Only the technology behind it is volatile.

items.name: Acting-party identity volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: how the system establishes whose list is being worked and who is working it. At the same time, a team member may be signed in through the web app, an agent may act on that team member's behalf through the agent surface, and a host workspace may pass in its own identity. The reference contract assumes a 'single user/session', but a team means each person needs their own list, reachable from any tab or device. WHY volatile: the team's identity mechanism (its sign-in provider, agent delegation tokens, host-supplied identity) is outside this system and differs per caller kind today. Delegated agent identity is also an area where conventions are still settling. LIKELIHOOD: high (three caller kinds already differ), with further change as the team's identity conventions evolve. EFFECT if unencapsulated: per-caller identity logic would leak into every list behavior. That risks one member's list being worked as another's, and makes adding a caller kind a change across the whole system.

items.name: Cross-surface consistency volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: how a change made on one surface becomes visible on the others, and how near-simultaneous changes to the same list are reconciled. A team member's agent can complete or clear todos while that member has the list open in a browser tab or an embedded host. The items-left count must stay correct after every change. WHY volatile: the mechanism (re-fetch on demand, polling, server push or host-mediated notification) depends on which surfaces are in use and what each host supports, and that set differs across members today. The reconciliation policy for concurrent toggle-all versus single-todo changes is also not fixed by the brief. LIKELIHOOD: medium-high. It becomes material as soon as agents and people work the same lists, which objective O5 makes a core aim. EFFECT if unencapsulated: freshness and conflict handling would be scattered across every surface and behavior, and items left and view contents would silently go stale or disagree between surfaces.

items.name: Hosting-environment volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: the environment the service runs in and how it is deployed, configured and restarted, following the team's house platform ('built the way we build everything else here'). WHY volatile: in-house platform conventions (container platform, configuration, secrets, rollout) usually change every 1 to 3 years, well inside the life of an everyday team tool. LIKELIHOOD: medium. EFFECT if unencapsulated: environment assumptions would leak into list keeping and the caller surfaces. A platform move would then risk the 'survives a service restart' guarantee and need code changes across the system. Expected disposition: operational concept rather than a component.

rejected.name: Reference-behavior scope volatility (due dates, priorities, tags, sharing, reordering, undo, offline)
rejected.reason: The founder and the reference contract explicitly put these out of scope, and the mission commits to 'decline anything beyond that well-known reference behavior'. Encapsulating for them would mean designing for a different product than this business is asking for.

rejected.name: List-behavior rule volatility (how capture, toggle all and clear completed work)
rejected.reason: The TodoMVC reference behavior is implemented identically by every app that follows it and is fixed by the mission. Changing it would change what the product is, and any encapsulation of it would be poor.

rejected.name: Wording-check rule volatility (what counts as blank)
rejected.reason: Whitespace-only versus meaningful wording is one predicate, shared by capture and reword. A conditional handles it, and it has no ripple effect.

rejected.name: View-set volatility (All / Active / Completed)
rejected.reason: A view is a predicate on the done flag. Adding or changing one is data or a conditional inside view selection, not an architectural change, and the reference fixes the set at three.

rejected.name: Toggle-all direction volatility
rejected.reason: The aggregate completion check is one conditional ('all done? then reopen all, else complete all').

rejected.name: Items-left counting volatility
rejected.reason: The remaining count is a single count of active todos across the list. Its freshness across surfaces is the real concern, and that is covered by Cross-surface consistency volatility.

rejected.name: Todo shape / schema volatility
rejected.reason: The shape is wording plus a done flag. Every extra attribute the brief hints at (dates, priority, tags) is explicitly declined, so schema growth assumes a change to the business that is not evidenced. Store-format change is covered by List-keeping technology volatility.

rejected.name: List ordering / reordering volatility
rejected.reason: Lists keep capture order and drag-to-reorder is explicitly out of scope. Nothing in the brief evidences a demand for other orderings.

rejected.name: Multi-user list sharing volatility
rejected.reason: Explicitly out of scope ('multi-user sharing'). Each team member keeps their own list, and per-member identity is covered by Acting-party identity volatility.

rejected.name: Offline-work volatility
rejected.reason: Offline sync is explicitly declined, and the mission deliberately keeps lists on the team's side rather than on the device.

rejected.name: Undo/redo history volatility
rejected.reason: Explicitly declined. The only 'undo' in the brief is reopening a todo or reversing toggle all, and both are fixed reference behaviors.

rejected.name: Edit-gesture volatility (Enter / Escape / blur / double-click)
rejected.reason: Which gestures commit or cancel a reword depends on the presentation host. This is the same underlying change as Presentation-host volatility.

rejected.name: Agent-tooling capability volatility (what agents may do on a list)
rejected.reason: The mission requires agents to get exactly the behavior a person gets. Any permission difference comes from who is acting on whose behalf, which is the same underlying change as Acting-party identity volatility.

rejected.name: Web-API style volatility (resource shapes, versioning)
rejected.reason: The shape of the web API is one instance of how callers reach the behaviors. Folded into Caller-protocol volatility.

rejected.name: Embedded UI protocol volatility (MCP Apps spec revisions)
rejected.reason: Revisions to the embedding protocol change how the experience is hosted. That is the same underlying change as Presentation-host volatility.

rejected.name: Persistence guarantee volatility (lists must survive restarts)
rejected.reason: Durable keeping is the whole point of the product ('no lost work') and will not change. Only the technology behind it varies, which is List-keeping technology volatility.

rejected.name: Team-size / load scaling volatility
rejected.reason: The customer is a small team trying the app out, and nothing evidences a jump in scale. If it comes, it is a scaling-policy choice in operational concepts, not an architectural seam.

rejected.name: Activity logging / audit block
rejected.reason: This would be a siren-song block (ch. 2 §3.6). Nothing in the brief asks for an audit trail of list changes, and no business volatility stands behind it.

rejected.name: Usage reporting / analytics block
rejected.reason: This would be a reflexive reporting block. The founder asks only for the always-visible items-left count, which is a list behavior, not reporting.

rejected.name: UI text localization volatility
rejected.reason: One team, with no mention of multiple languages. Pluralizing 'items left' or translating labels is formatter or resource-table work, not structural.

rejected.name: Storage-location regulation volatility (data residency)
rejected.reason: An internal todo tool for one small team, with no regulatory or multi-market evidence. Any change of where data lives is already covered by List-keeping technology volatility.

decisions.essenceRationale: Working a list (capture, reword, discard, complete/reopen, toggle all, clear completed) is the one thing every team member and every agent acting for them comes to this product to do. It is the fixed reference behavior the mission commits to and will not grow. It stays the same whether the caller is a person in the web app, a person in a host workspace, or agent tooling, and whatever store keeps the list. The product's differentiator is not the verbs themselves. It is that one kept, team-side list behaves identically to every party and every surface, with each change landing once and showing everywhere. That abstraction, a new name not in the founder's list, subsumes six raw requests and the agent-tooling request.

decisions.essenceRationale: Every party that comes back to a list first needs that same list recalled exactly as it was left: the same wording, order and done states, whatever tab, device, host or agent they come from. They then look at it through a view, with a true count of what remains. The guarantee that the list is kept and recalled on the team's side and seen identically everywhere is why the founder wants a real service rather than a browser toy. It does not change over time and is shared by every member and agent. It subsumes three raw requests (switch views, see items left, find my list next time) and the embedded-host request under one abstraction that reads but never changes the list.

listAccess.title: ListAccess — atomic kept-list verbs over one member's durable todo list (ResourceAccess, Postgres binding). Callers: ListManager only, sync. Every op is scoped to exactly one member; nothing reaches across members. No events, no queued ops, no Temporal. Durability: an acknowledged change is committed before the op returns; reads see every acknowledged change (read-your-writes). Bulk ops (SettleAll, SweepCompleted) are applied in one store transaction, never half-applied. Store technology and its binding (connection, credentials from hosting configuration/secrets) are hidden behind this contract.

ListFault.description: Error model. Every op returns a Go error whose kind is one of these values; store-specific errors never leak. todoNotFound (terminal): ReviseWording/SettleCompletion named a todoId absent from the member's list — ListManager decides how to reconcile (e.g. another surface removed it). todoIdConflict (terminal): AppendTodo retried a todoId already kept with different wording. invalidRequest (terminal): empty memberId or todoId. storeUnavailable (transient, retry-safe): the store could not be reached or the transaction aborted; nothing was applied. Idempotency: AppendTodo is idempotent on todoId (same id + same wording returns the kept todo); ReviseWording, SettleCompletion, SettleAll, SweepCompleted are idempotent by nature; WithdrawTodo of an absent todo succeeds. Orchestration guidance (non-normative): 5s per-call timeout, retry storeUnavailable only.

Member.description: The team member whose list is worked, as resolved by IdentityAccess.recognizeActingParty and passed through by ListManager. memberId is an opaque, stable identifier; ListAccess keys every list on it and never interprets it. An empty memberId is rejected (ListFault invalidRequest, terminal).

memberId.description: Opaque stable member identifier from IdentityAccess.

Todo.description: One kept todo: its id, wording and done flag. The shape is fixed (no dates, priority, tags, ordering, sharing). Lists are returned in capture order (the order AppendTodo first accepted each todoId).

done.description: true when the todo is done (completed), false when active.

todoId.description: Caller-minted id (ListManager mints it, e.g. a UUID, before the first AppendTodo attempt so retries are recognisable). Unique within a member's list.

wording.description: The todo's wording, stored verbatim. ListAccess applies no blank-wording or trimming rule; that is ListManager's.

identityAccess.title: identityAccess contract

ActingParty.description: The party working the list, in business terms. No provider claim shapes cross this boundary.

ActingPartyKind.description: Who is working the member's list: self (the member in person through the web app), agentTooling (agent tooling acting on the member's behalf through ListApi or ListMcpServer), hostWorkspace (the member working through the list embedded in a host workspace). No committed behavior varies by it today; it is reported so ListManager can carry it, not to branch list rules on it.

CallerProof.description: The proof of identity the caller presented, forwarded by ListManager exactly as the client received it (web-app sign-in session/bearer credential, agent delegation token, or host-workspace-supplied identity assertion). Opaque to ListManager and the clients: they never parse it, never tag it with a caller kind and never add a member identifier of their own. Only this component interprets it. It is an object so that a future proof element can be added without changing the signature.

credential.description: The credential string verbatim, without any transport prefix such as 'Bearer '. Empty means the caller presented no proof, which is a recognition failure (Auth), not a misuse. Never logged, never echoed in errors or results.

MemberID.description: Opaque, stable identifier of the team member whose list is worked, as resolved by the team's identity provider. The same member yields the same MemberID whichever caller kind presented the proof (signed in directly, agent tooling on their behalf, or a host workspace). ListManager passes it on to ListAccess as the list owner and must not parse it. Never empty in a successful result.

RecognizedParty.description: The recognized result: whose list is being worked (member) and who is working it (actingParty). Returned only when the provider has verified the proof and resolved the member it acts for; there is no partial or default result.

identityAccess.notes:
# IdentityAccess: detailed design

Status: IN-DESIGN. The App C section 6 check is complete, but no system-architect has reviewed this yet. Review happens at the activity's gate. Do not construct against this contract until that review passes; FROZEN is not claimed here.

Designed to the senior-developer standard (the default hand-off; state records no named assignment). Reviewer: system-architect.

Facet: recognize the acting party behind a list request. One contract on this service. Sole caller: ListManager, synchronous, once per list request before any ListAccess call (step a0 of every dynamic view, uc1 to uc13). Sole downstream: TeamIdentityProvider (Resource, external, reached over HTTP). No queued operations, no events, no Temporal.

## Operation

RecognizeActingParty(callerProof) -> RecognizedParty. Verifies the proof against TeamIdentityProvider and resolves the member it acts for, then reports that member and the acting party (self, agentTooling, hostWorkspace). It has no side effects in this system. It returns a result only when the provider has verified the proof; otherwise it returns an error and no member (fail closed, R4). The result is the same for the same member whichever surface the proof came through (R3).

Pre-condition: none beyond the parameter shape. Post-condition: a returned member is one the provider has verified this proof acts for. Never a caller-asserted identifier, never a default member, never a guessed member.

## Decisions on the scope note's open questions

- Q1 Proof shape: one opaque proof (CallerProof.credential), not tagged by caller kind. Tagging would make ListManager and the clients know the caller kinds and change when a new kind appears, which is the volatility this component exists to absorb. This component tells the kinds apart itself, from what the provider verifies (session vs delegation token vs host assertion). CallerProof is an object so a future proof element can be added without a signature change.
- Q2 Acting party: minimal. ActingParty carries only kind. No agent identity, no host name, no provider claims. Adding a field later is additive.
- Q3 Failure taxonomy: proof rejected (Auth), provider unavailable (Infrastructure, Transient or RateLimited), misuse (ContractMisuse). See Error model. These are the outcomes ListManager has to tell apart to report honestly rather than as not signed in.
- Q4 Host-supplied identity: accepted only as a provider-verifiable assertion. A host-passed member identifier that the provider has not verified is a rejection (Auth). If the team's host conventions need a provider-side exchange, that exchange happens inside this component and the contract does not change.
- Q5 Caching: none in this construction. Every call verifies with the provider, so revocation takes effect at once. If latency demands it later, a short-lived cache keyed by a hash of the credential and bounded by the proof's expiry can be added inside the component without a contract change; see Review questions.
- Q6 Which provider: not named in the committed basis. The contract is provider-neutral; infra is ExternalHTTP. Endpoint, client credentials and the delegation-token convention come from configuration. See Review questions.

## Idempotency

Read-only with respect to this system: no state is written, so a repeat call is safe and needs no key. The same proof gives the same member while the provider still accepts it. After expiry or revocation the same proof gives Auth.

## Error model

Use the framework resourceaccess.Error kinds.

- Auth (terminal): proof rejected. Covers empty credential (no proof presented), malformed, expired, revoked, unverifiable or unresolvable proof, a proof that resolves to no member, and a host- or agent-asserted member the provider has not verified. The error must not reveal which of these occurred to the caller beyond a generic reason; Detail may say 'not recognized' only.
- Infrastructure (retryable): TeamIdentityProvider unreachable or answering 5xx. This is distinguishable from Auth so the Manager and clients can report provider unavailable, not not signed in.
- Transient (retryable): a timeout or interrupted request to the provider.
- RateLimited (retryable): the provider throttled this component (429).
- ContractMisuse (terminal): this component's own provider configuration is missing or invalid, or a credential exceeds 16 KiB or contains bytes that cannot be a credential (NUL). A provider response this component cannot interpret is Infrastructure, not Auth, so a provider fault never reads as the user being signed out.

NotFound, Conflict, QuotaExhausted and ContentPolicy are not used.

No credential, token fragment, provider response body, client secret or endpoint URL with secrets may reach the error text, logs or traces. Log only the outcome kind and, on success, the acting-party kind.

## Security

- Fail closed on every path; an error is never accompanied by a member.
- Trust only what the provider verifies. Signature, issuer, audience and expiry checks (or the provider's introspection answer) are required before a member is returned.
- For agentTooling, the member is the one the delegation is verified to act for, never a member the agent names.
- Provider secrets and endpoints come from the hosting environment's configuration, never code.

## Orchestration guidance (non-normative)

Advisory timeout, as a design estimate: 3 seconds per call (it sits on every list request). Retry only retryable kinds, at most twice with a short backoff; never retry Auth. ListManager picks the actual policy.

## Internal structure (for the constructor; not contract)

In internal/resourceaccess/identity: an HTTP implementation of IdentityAccess fronting TeamIdentityProvider.

- A small provider client (verify proof, resolve member) behind an internal interface, so the provider can be swapped or doubled in tests.
- A recognizer that classifies the verified proof into self, agentTooling or hostWorkspace and maps provider claims to MemberID. Provider claim names stay in this package.
- An error classifier mapping HTTP status and transport failures to the kinds above.

Test against an httptest double of the provider. Cover: signed-in member (self), agent on behalf of a member (agentTooling), host-supplied identity (hostWorkspace), the same member through all three giving the same MemberID, empty credential, malformed and expired proof, proof for member A with a host- or agent-asserted member B (must give A or Auth, never B), provider 5xx and unreachable (Infrastructure), timeout (Transient), 429 (RateLimited), an uninterpretable provider response (Infrastructure), and that no credential appears in any error or log.

## Factoring

One operation: the System commits exactly one atomic business verb for this component (recognizeActingParty) and every dynamic view calls only that. Rejected:
- A separate VerifyProof and ResolveMember pair: it would let a caller hold a verified proof without a member, or a member without a verified proof, and would leak the provider's two-step shape.
- Per-caller-kind ops (RecognizeMember, RecognizeAgent, RecognizeHost): they push the caller-kind volatility up into ListManager.
- An authorization op (CanWork(member, list)): no multi-user sharing exists; rejected as speculative in the scope note.
- Member profile lookup: no view calls it.

Reuse test: a second team fronting a different identity provider (or a new delegation convention) would implement this contract unchanged. Nothing in the signature or $defs names the provider or its claims.

## App C section 6 standard check

- 1 Reusable: PASS.
- 2a At least 2 ops: WAIVED at 1. The System commits a single atomic verb for this component and TP-OP-REACHED forbids ops no dynamic view calls. Recognition is one indivisible act (verify and resolve together, fail closed); splitting it would create a weaker, leakier contract. The single op takes a whole-object parameter and returns a whole-object result, so it is not too coarse in the App B 5.2 sense.
- 2b 3 to 5 ops: WAIVED at 1, same justification.
- 2c At most 12: PASS.
- 2d Under 20: PASS.
- 3 No property-like ops: PASS. RecognizeActingParty is a behavioural verb, not a GetX on stored state.
- 4 At most 2 contracts: PASS (1).
- 5 Not a junior hand-off and 6 Architect or senior designer: PASS on the senior-developer default. State records no named hand-off assignment; the activity's junior-developer worker class applies to construction. The architect must confirm this at review, since both items are non-waivable.

Layer rules: ResourceAccess called only by a Manager, no queued ops, no events, no Temporal, one Resource behind it: PASS.

## Review questions for system-architect

- Provider: confirm the concrete TeamIdentityProvider and its protocol (OIDC token validation vs introspection) and the agent delegation-token convention before construction; they drive the learning-curve risk named in the scope note.
- Host identity: confirm the MCP Apps host passes a provider-verifiable assertion; if it needs a provider-side exchange, confirm that exchange may live here.
- ActingParty: confirm kind alone is enough for ListManager, and that ListManager does not need the agent's own identity for anything committed.
- Caching: confirm no caching for the trial, given a 3 second budget on every list request.
- C-list-manager: its contract must forward the client's credential verbatim as CallerProof, use RecognizedParty.member as ListAccess's list owner, and map Auth to not recognized and Infrastructure/Transient/RateLimited to identity provider unavailable.
- Hand-off: confirm items 5 and 6 above.

messageBus.title: messageBus contract

Audience.description: Opaque key of the one party a message may reach. For ListChanged it is the acting member's identifier as ListManager received it from IdentityAccess. The bus never parses it. It only compares it for exact equality, so a message can only ever reach consumers bound to the same Audience. Empty is ContractMisuse.

Body.description: The notice's content, serialized by the publisher (for ListChanged: the member's itemsLeft count). The bus carries it byte for byte and never reads it. At most 64 KiB of valid UTF-8; anything else is ContractMisuse. May be empty.

Message.description: One notice handed to the bus: its kind, the one audience it may reach, and its opaque body. This is the whole envelope; the bus has no list-domain types.

MessageKind.description: Names what kind of notice a message is, e.g. "ListChanged". The publisher picks it; the bus never interprets it, so a new kind needs no change to the bus. Must be non-empty, at most 64 bytes, letters and digits only; anything else is ContractMisuse.

# MessageBus: detailed design

Status: IN-DESIGN. The App C section 6 check below is complete, but no system-architect has reviewed this yet. Review happens at the activity's gate. Do not construct against this contract until that review passes; FROZEN is not claimed here.

Designed to the senior-developer standard (the default under the senior hand-off model). Reviewer: system-architect. Construction worker class: junior-developer.

Layer: Utility. Facet: carry a notice from the party that publishes it toward the one audience it concerns, without interpreting it. One contract on this service. Sole caller: ListManager, synchronous (UC1 "Work a list" step a9 and UC9 "Let our agent tooling drive the list" step a3, label publish(ListChanged(member, itemsLeft))). No outbound edges and no Resource, so no infra. No queued operations and no Temporal, since this is a Utility.

## Operation

Publish(message Message) error
- Pre-condition: message.kind and message.audience are non-empty and valid, and message.body is within its limits (see $defs).
- Behaviour: synchronous accept-and-hand-off. It returns once the transport has accepted the message, not once any consumer has received it. Publish never blocks on a consumer. With no consumer bound to that audience, which is the case today because the committed design declares none, it returns nil and the message is dropped. That is not an error.
- Isolation: a message is only ever delivered to consumers bound to exactly message.audience. The bus never delivers across audiences and never stores or replays messages, so it cannot become a side channel into another member's list.
- Ordering: messages that one caller publishes in sequence for the same audience are delivered in that order. No ordering is promised across audiences.
- Side effects: none on list state. The bus has no dependency on ListAccess, a store, or list types.
- Default transport: in-process fan-out. Swapping to a broker or a host-mediated notification channel changes only the implementation behind this contract, never ListManager.

For ListManager, a ListChanged publish is Message{kind: "ListChanged", audience: <member>, body: <serialized itemsLeft>}. The ListChanged shape is ListManager's to own.

## Error model

- ContractMisuse (terminal; do not retry): the message is invalid (empty or malformed kind, empty audience, or a body over 64 KiB or not valid UTF-8). Nothing is handed off.
- Unavailable (transient; a retry may succeed): the transport could not accept the message, for example because the bus is shut down or a future broker is unreachable. Nothing is handed off.
- Consumer-side failures never surface to the publisher.

Guidance for the caller (non-normative): the list change has already been applied durably before the publish. ListManager should treat a publish failure as best-effort propagation: log it, do not undo the change, and do not fail the member's request. Keep Publish well under 50 ms in-process. It must not noticeably delay the change.

## Delivery and idempotency

At-most-once. Publish is not deduplicated: publishing the same message twice delivers it twice to any bound consumer. A ListChanged notice carries current state (the latest items-left count), so a consumer that sees a duplicate or misses one is corrected by the next notice. A future consumer must tolerate duplicates.

## Factoring decisions

- Business-agnostic envelope (kind, audience, opaque body) instead of a ListChanged type. A Utility must not know the list domain, and new message kinds must not change the bus (scope note, Extensibility).
- Rejected for now: a Subscribe or Receive operation. No dynamic view calls one and no component has a consumer edge, so methodcheck TP-OP-REACHED would reject it, and adding one would invent consumers. When the architecture adds a consumer edge (for example from a surface's Manager or Client), Subscribe(audience) is factored in as a second operation on this same facet, and the audience-isolation rule above already constrains it.
- Rejected: a separate typed operation per message kind (PublishListChanged). That would be feature-named (Directive 4) and would grow with every kind.

## Reuse review

Any team building a notice bus for some other domain (orders, documents) would implement Publish(Message) unchanged. Nothing in it names todos, lists, members or a transport technology.

## App C section 6 standard check

| # | Guideline | Status | Justification |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Reusable | PASS | Generic envelope, no domain or transport leakage |
| 2a | Not a single operation | WAIVED | The committed design has exactly one call into this component, publish(ListChanged), in UC1 a9 and UC9 a3. Every other candidate operation (Subscribe, Unsubscribe, Flush) is uncalled, and TP-OP-REACHED rejects uncalled ops. The operation is not too coarse; the component's committed surface is one verb. To be revisited when a consumer edge is added. |
| 2b | 3-5 operations | WAIVED | Same reason as 2a |
| 2c | 12 operations or fewer | PASS | 1 |
| 2d | Fewer than 20 operations | PASS | 1 |
| 3 | No property-like ops | PASS | Publish is behavioural |
| 4 | 1 or 2 contracts per service | PASS | 1 |
| 5 | Not a junior hand-off | PASS | Designed to the senior-developer standard; juniors construct only |
| 6 | Architect or senior designer | PASS | Senior-developer design; system-architect review |

## Open questions for architect review

1. Operational concepts are not committed. This contract assumes sync, in-process, at-most-once delivery with best-effort propagation. Confirm or amend this when .operationalConcepts is committed.
2. Consumers: the design has no subscriber of MessageBus, so today a publish reaches no one. Decide whether surfaces (ListApp, ListApi, ListMcpServer) or their Managers subscribe. That needs an architecture amendment plus a Subscribe operation here.
3. Coverage: only UC1 and UC9 publish. UC3 to UC8 end without a publish. Is that intended for ListManager? It does not affect this contract.

# ListAccess — Requirements scope note (activity C-list-access)

Scope capture only. This note says what ListAccess must do, who calls it and which quality bars it must clear. It proposes no operations, signatures or contract shape; that is Detailed Design's job.

## 1. Position in the committed design
- Layer: ResourceAccess (component id `list-access`, contract key `listAccess`).
- Encapsulates **List-keeping technology volatility**: the technology and location where every team member's list is durably kept on the team's side. The store is expected to change at least once (a simple store for 'try it tomorrow', then the team's standard managed database).
- Encapsulates **Hosting-environment volatility**, but only at the store binding: how the store is located, configured and reached in the house platform. The committed design assigns the rest of that volatility to the operational concept.
- The committed atomic business verbs are appendTodo, reviseWording, withdrawTodo, settleCompletion, settleAll, sweepCompleted, recallList and countItemsLeft. They are listed here as the committed vocabulary the responsibilities below trace to. Detailed Design owns their final shape.

## 2. Callers and downstream
- **Only caller: ListManager** (sync, relationship `list-manager → list-access`). No client, engine or other ResourceAccess calls ListAccess. Clients (ListApp, ListApi, ListMcpServer) reach it only through ListManager.
- **Only downstream: ListStore** (Resource, sync, relationship `list-access → list-store`, label 'append / revise / withdraw / settle / sweep / read member's list entries (idempotency: todo id)').
- No relationship to MessageBus, IdentityAccess or TeamIdentityProvider. ListAccess neither publishes nor recognizes callers. ListManager publishes ListChanged and resolves the acting member before it calls ListAccess.

## 3. Responsibilities (each traced to a committed edge)
Every request is scoped to one **member's** list. ListManager supplies the member after IdentityAccess has recognized the caller.

| # | Responsibility | Traces to (dynamic view · step) |
|---|---|---|
| R1 | Append a new active todo at the end of the member's list, preserving capture order. Idempotent on the todo id. | uc1 a2; uc3 a1; uc9 a1 |
| R2 | Overwrite one todo's wording. Idempotent. | uc1 a3; uc4 a1; uc9 a1 |
| R3 | Remove one todo. Idempotent: removing an already-removed todo is not an error to the store. | uc1 a3b, a4; uc4 b1 (reword to blank → removal); uc5 a1; uc9 a1 |
| R4 | Set one todo's done flag to a given state. Idempotent. | uc1 a5; uc6 a1; uc9 a1 |
| R5 | Set every todo in the member's list to done, or every one to not done. Idempotent. ListManager picks the direction; ListAccess does not decide toggle-all direction. | uc1 a6, a6b; uc7 a1, b1; uc9 a1 |
| R6 | Remove every done todo and leave active todos untouched. Idempotent. | uc1 a7; uc8 a1; uc9 a1 |
| R7 | Return the member's todos (wording and done flag) in capture order. | uc1 d6, d7; uc2 a1; uc7 d1; uc8 d1; uc10 a1; uc12 a1; uc13 a1 |
| R8 | Return the count of active (not done) todos across the member's whole list, regardless of which view the caller is showing. | uc1 a8; uc2 a2; uc3–uc8 a2; uc9 a2; uc10 a2; uc11 a1; uc12 a2; uc13 a2 |
| R9 | Keep lists durably on the team's side so they survive closing, restarting the service, and switching tab or device. Never rely on browser-held state. | uc12 (find my list still there); List-keeping technology volatility; Hosting-environment volatility (B-09 trace) |
| R10 | Hide the store technology and its binding from ListManager. Changing ListStore's technology or hosting binding must not change ListManager or anything above it. | component `encapsulates`; List-keeping technology + Hosting-environment volatilities |

Explicitly **not** ListAccess's job (these belong to ListManager by the committed design):
- Choosing toggle-all direction (the 'all done?' conditional is fed by R7).
- Applying the blank-wording rule or turning a blank reword into a removal.
- Filtering for the All / Active / Completed views (a view is a predicate over R7's result).
- Sequencing a change with its items-left recount, and publishing ListChanged.
- Recognizing who is acting.
- Reconciling concurrent changes across surfaces (Cross-surface consistency volatility).

## 4. Non-functional constraints
**Maintainability**
- Speak in kept-list business terms ('todo', 'member's list', 'done'), not store terms (rows, documents, keys, SQL). Per the Method, a ResourceAccess exposes atomic business verbs, never CRUD/IO.
- Each verb is atomic. ListAccess holds no business sequencing and never calls another component at its own layer or above.

**Extensibility**
- At least two store bindings are expected over the system's life. A new binding must be addable without touching ListManager. Detailed Design should plan a binding-agnostic test suite that each binding passes.
- The todo shape is fixed at wording plus done flag (schema growth was rejected as speculative). Do not gold-plate for dates, priority, tags, ordering, sharing, undo or offline. All of these are declined.

**Security / isolation**
- One member's list must never be read or changed as another's. Every responsibility is scoped by the member ListManager supplies, and nothing ListAccess exposes may reach across members. (The Acting-party identity volatility rationale names this risk.)
- Store credentials and connection details come from the hosting environment's configuration and secrets. They are never hard-coded and never pass through callers.

**Reliability / correctness**
- 'No lost work': an acknowledged change must be durable before it returns.
- Idempotency, as the committed edges require: R1 on the todo id, and R2–R6 by their nature. Retries from ListManager must be safe.
- R7 must keep capture order, and R8 must equal the number of not-done todos R7 would return at the same moment.
- Bulk changes (R5, R6) must not leave a member's list half-applied in a way a later read could observe as inconsistent.

**Performance / scale**
- Load is a small team trying the app out (scaling volatility rejected as speculative), so no special throughput bar applies. Calls are synchronous and on the user's interaction path, so keep latency at ordinary interactive levels.

## 5. Full scope of the activity (beyond coding)
The activity list has C-list-access at 10 days, junior-developer, risk bucket 2. Scope includes: the learning curve for the first store binding; integration with ListStore; a test client and a test plan that exercise R1–R10, including idempotent retries, member isolation and restart-survival; and component documentation.

## 6. Open questions for Detailed Design
1. **Operational concepts are not committed.** The Deployment & Operations Model (slot 6) was not available when this note was written. The concrete first store and its hosting binding (how configuration and secrets reach ListAccess) must be confirmed from it before Detailed Design fixes the binding.
2. **Who mints the todo id.** R1 must be idempotent on the todo id. Detailed Design must decide whether ListManager supplies it (enabling retry-safe appends) or ListAccess/ListStore assigns it, and how a retried append is recognized.
3. **Missing-todo semantics.** How R2 and R4 report a todo that no longer exists (for example, an agent cleared it while a person was rewording it), given that cross-surface reconciliation belongs to ListManager.
4. **Atomicity across a change and its recount.** ListManager calls a change and then R8 separately. Decide whether ListAccess must guarantee read-your-writes between consecutive calls (it should, for 'items left stays correct after every change'), and what the consistency expectation is under concurrent surfaces.
5. **The setting for R5.** The committed edges carry the target state (done or not done). Confirm that the direction stays with ListManager and is never inferred by ListAccess.
6. **Member key form.** The form of the member identity that IdentityAccess produces and ListAccess keys lists on, coordinated with the C-identity-access activity.
7. **Failure vocabulary.** How store unavailability is surfaced to ListManager without leaking store-specific errors (R10).

ListAccess integration (activity C-list-access).

Integration scope (committed system design): ListAccess is a ResourceAccess leaf. Inbound: list-manager -> list-access (sync; appendTodo/reviseWording/withdrawTodo/settleCompletion/settleAll/sweepCompleted/recallList/countItemsLeft). Outbound: list-access -> list-store (sync; Postgres). Every dynamic view that crosses ListAccess (uc1-uc13) uses only these two edges, so this activity integrates exactly one neighbor: the ListStore Resource. The ListManager edge is integrated by the ListManager activity (the Manager builds the composition root); no cmd/server exists yet and none was hand-made here.

Wiring: the store binding is the generated public constructor todolist.NewPostgresListAccess(ctx, *pgxpool.Pool). The pool comes from the platform Postgres pool constructor (framework-go-infrastructure-postgres NewPool), and the constructor ensures its own schema idempotently (todo_list_item keyed by member_id+todo_id, ordered by an identity seq for capture order). No frozen contract, test plan or generated file was changed.

Scenario hooks (internal/resourceaccess/todolist/access_hooks_test.go): newSubject builds the real Postgres-backed ListAccess through NewPostgresListAccess on a throwaway Postgres testcontainer per scenario (framework-go-infrastructure-postgres/testinfra.StartPostgres), so each scenario starts from an empty, isolated kept list. The hooks import rule allows only stdlib, the component, scenariohost and testinfra, so a per-scenario schema on the host's shared Postgres URL could not be used. Every hooked step arranges the bound starting list (t1 'A' open, then t2 'B' done for member m) through the component's own verbs (AppendTodo, SettleCompletion) with host-served ResourceAccess call contexts, then calls the bound operation. No mocks or fakes stand in for any component. No other _test.go files exist in the package. go.mod now requires framework-go-scenariohost v0.4.0, which the generated scenarios file needs.

Run status: the final full run_checks passed 65/65, including arch, gofmt, lint, the generated-test drift check and all 57 listAccess scenarios against real Postgres. No plan defects.
